title: Research
text: Answering this question requires choosing a strategy to handle intercurrent events. My dissertation work is about composite strategy, and for binary endpoints this answer is easy — the event is just another failure. For continuous endpoints it is trickier: what value represents failure? And what are the consequences of choosing this value?

title: Research
text:
Patients who experience an ICE
Suppose a respiratory trial measures FEV1, or how much air a patient can force out of their lungs in one second. It is a continuous number, in liters, and at the end you compare the average in the treated group to the average in the control group.
Trials can be messy. Some patients stop taking the drug, some need rescue medication, some die. These are called intercurrent events, and they leave you holding a set of patients with no usable endpoint measurement.
Dropping them would be throwing away information. The patients who leave a trial are often the ones doing worst, so analyzing only the ones who stayed makes almost any drug look better than it is. The composite strategy — one of five approaches set out in the ICH E9 (R1) regulatory guidance — takes the opposite position: leaving the trial is itself part of the outcome. When the outcome is continuous, assign those patients a failure value and analyze everyone together.
That creates a question: what failure value should you use?

title: Research
text:
The issues with current practice
There is no hard rule on how to choose this value. The common practice varies across trials. Some pick something that sounded appropriately bad: zero, or the worst result anyone in the trial recorded. Two things go wrong with these options.
The first is that it cannot be defended. As Bell and colleagues put it in a 2025 presentation, there is no principled reason failure should be −16 units rather than −17, for example. The number ends up looking like a choice the sponsor made, because it is.
The second is that it has statistical consequences. Assigning a quarter of your patients an extreme value creates a two-humped distribution. The variance of the endpoint inflates, and the sample size needed to detect a real effect can rise several-fold — enough to make a trial infeasible.



Illustrative. Simulated data, not trial results. Both panels show the same patients with the same 25% intercurrent event rate; only the assigned failure value differs. Pushing failure out to an extreme more than doubles the spread of the analyzed outcome, and that spread is what drives sample size.


A recent proposal by Bell et al. repairs the arbitrariness: define the failure value relative to the control population — say, the 10th percentile of patients on standard of care. Now it carries a clinical interpretation, and it sits inside the range of outcomes real patients actually have.

title: Research
section: The part that motivated my dissertation
text:
The part that motivated my dissertation
That percentile is a property of a population nobody can observe. It has to be estimated from the control patients in your own trial, which means the failure value is not a known constant. It is an estimate, and it therefore carries uncertainty of its own.
Writing it down makes the issue plain. Each patient’s analyzed outcome is
\[
y_i^{*} = \begin{cases} y_i & \text{if the patient completed} \\ \upsilon & \text{if an intercurrent event occurred} \end{cases}
\]
and under a quantile definition the failure value is
\[
\upsilon = \nu + \Phi^{-1}(q)\,\omega ,
\]
where \(\nu\) and \(\omega\) are the mean and standard deviation of outcomes among control patients, and \(q\) is the chosen percentile.
Without a variance correction, you would estimate \(\nu\) and \(\omega\), plug them in, and carry on as though \(\upsilon\) were exact. That understates how much you don’t know. Intervals come out too narrow, and the trial reports more certainty than it earned.
This is where a Bayesian treatment does real work rather than decorative work. Treat \(\nu\) and \(\omega\) as unknown quantities with prior distributions, and uncertainty about the failure value propagates through to the treatment effect on its own — no separate variance correction required.

title: Research
text:
Two estimators
We developed two approaches, and they are genuinely different tools rather than one better and one worse.




Two-stage estimator
Parametric joint model




How it works
Stage one estimates the failure value from control completers. Stage two carries its entire posterior — not a single number — into the treatment effect, by Bayesian multiple imputation.
Models the outcome and the occurrence of intercurrent events at once, then recovers the marginal effect by G-computation: predict every patient under each arm, average, difference.


What it assumes
Nothing about why patients left the trial.
A specified model for dropout, including which covariates drive it.


Strongest when
The dropout mechanism is poorly understood, robustness has to be demonstrated, or the control arm is small enough to want historical data through the prior.
Dropout is plausibly explained by observed covariates, baseline correlates strongly with outcome, and power is the design priority.


The trade
Widest intervals of any method tested — it buys stability with precision.
Coverage slips modestly when dropout rates are severely lopsided between arms.



Both share the property that matters: uncertainty in the failure value propagates on its own, through posterior sampling, rather than needing a variance correction bolted on afterwards.

title: Research
text:
What the simulations showed
I evaluated both against four frequentist benchmarks across more than 120 scenarios, 5,000 replications each.
The joint model was consistently the more efficient of the two. Under a modest true effect and 30% dropout in both arms, it reached 80% power with roughly 225 patients per arm, against 282 to 293 for every other method tested — about a fifth fewer patients, which is real money and real time.



Patients per arm required for 80% power, under dropout that depends only on observed information. From the simulation study; a modest true effect of 0.09 L with 30% intercurrent event rates in both arms.


The two-stage estimator was the more robust of the two. It held interval coverage near its nominal level across a wide range of conditions, including non-normal outcomes and dropout that depended on the very outcome that went unmeasured. It buys that stability with wider intervals, which makes the choice between the two a genuine trade rather than a ranking.

Two caveats I would want a reader to take away with the results.
The efficiency gain belongs to the joint model’s structure — estimating the failure value and the treatment effect together, from the full sample.
The two-stage model is more similar in structure to the frequentist alternatives. It also requires fewer assumptions and only puts priors on the control group, which may make it friendlier to regulatory agencies.

title: Research
section: The other half of the dissertation
text:
The other half of the dissertation
An earlier chapter deals with preclinical pharmacokinetics. In small-animal studies each animal is often measured once and then sacrificed, so no single subject has a complete concentration-time curve, which complicates estimating drug exposure and the quantities derived from it.
The problem I took up there is one of prior specification. Existing Bayesian approaches put an inverse-Wishart prior on the covariance matrix. It is convenient and conjugate, but it does not let you separate what you believe about the variances from what you believe about the correlation between compartments. This is an issue especially if you believe you are using noninformative priors when in fact you are not. The two are bound together by the structure of the prior, so it is impossible to be noninformative about both at the same time — and in a design this data-poor, the prior carries real weight in the inference.



Standard deviations colored by correlation for different covariance matrix prior options. Under the inverse-Wishart, the two are visibly linked. The LKJ specification leaves them independent.


An LKJ prior on the correlation, with separate priors on the standard deviations, removes the entanglement and lets each component be specified independently. A second addition — a regression-based prior encoding the biological relationship between plasma and tissue concentrations — brings genuine information to a design that carries very little data per animal. Both sharpened inference, with the clearest gains in bioequivalence assessment and when tissue measurements were incomplete.

title: Projects
section: Finding lead pipes that nobody has records for
text:
Finding lead pipes that nobody has records for
Utilities are required to inventory their water service lines and replace the old ones made of lead. The difficulty is that records from the early twentieth century are patchy. A city can end up knowing the material of some of its lines but unsure about thousands of others — and digging up an unknown line to find out costs time, labor, and money.
Working through Baylor’s Statistical Consulting Center, a fellow graduate student and I took on this problem for a municipal water utility. The data covered more than 14,000 service lines. About 8,400 had a known material; roughly 6,000 did not. The question was which of the unknowns were likely to be, or to have once been, lead.
The statistical process. One predictor turned out to be a perfect predictor. Every line known to contain lead sat on a block where another lead line had also been confirmed — the predictor separated the outcome perfectly. The issue with that is that ordinary logistic regression cannot cope with complete separation: the likelihood has no interior maximum, coefficients run off toward infinity, and standard errors become huge and meaningless. We fit Firth logistic regression instead, which penalizes the score equations using a term derived from Jeffreys’ prior. It shrinks estimates toward zero and returns usable, stable inference in exactly this situation. Conventional logistic regression predicted about as well, but its parameter estimates were unusable.



Illustrative. Synthetic data showing the situation, not the project’s own records. When one predictor divides the outcome cleanly, an unpenalized fit keeps pushing its coefficient upward without ever settling. Firth’s penalty, derived from Jeffreys’ prior, pulls the estimate back to a finite value with a usable standard error.


Building the features. Four predictors were chosen: the year the structure was built, the material of the nearest neighboring line, whether a lead line was confirmed on the same block, and each line’s distance from the geographic center of the known lead lines. Missing construction years were filled in by multiple imputation with predictive mean matching, and the continuous predictors were standardized.
Validating it. We fit all sixteen combinations of the four predictors and assessed each by five-fold cross-validation, stratified so every fold carried a representative share of the rare positive cases. Because the cost of missing a lead line is far higher than the cost of investigating a clean one, we classified at a deliberately conservative threshold rather than the default. Every model containing the block-level predictor identified all known lead lines with no false negatives and no false positives at that threshold.



Fitted coefficients from the recommended model, with 95% profile-penalized likelihood intervals. Two predictors carry the signal; the other two are retained for prediction despite intervals that cross zero.


What came out of it. Applied to the unknown lines, the recommended model flagged 306 as likely to be or to have been lead — meaning roughly 95% of the unknown lines could be deprioritized rather than excavated. Our job was not to make the final call — that rests with the regulator — but to build the strongest case the data could support for where replacement effort should go. The flagged lines clustered in the older parts of the city, next to the lead lines already on record, which is what you would hope to see from a model that has learned something real.
The broader lesson is that the default model won’t always fit the problem, and the failure is usually informative. Here the variable that broke the fit was the best predictor we had, so the right response was to change the estimation method rather than drop the variable.

Joint work with a fellow graduate student, under the direction of two faculty statisticians. The underlying service line data belongs to the utility and is not reproduced here; the description above covers method and aggregate findings only.

title: Projects
section: Fault detection in a water treatment trailer
text:
Fault detection in a water treatment trailer
I spent a summer as a Data Science Fellow in the MoWaTER program, an NSF-supported collaboration between Baylor University and the Colorado School of Mines. Our subject was a mobile Direct Potable Reuse trailer: a self-contained treatment train that takes municipal wastewater and turns it into drinking water, about 7,000 gallons a day, while doubling as a public demonstration of what sustainable water treatment looks like.
The trailer is heavily instrumented. Between 165 and 193 sensors record pressure, flow, and power every thirty seconds, across 71 operating sessions ranging from an hour to nineteen days. The operators wanted something specific from all that data: a way to characterize regular operating conditions, and secondly how to detect faults in the system.
The shape of the data. Both processes we focused on are cyclic. They run, then a backwash reverses the flow to clear accumulated debris, then they run again. So the natural unit of analysis is not a time point but a cycle — one complete stretch of operation between backwashes. We split the record into cycles, discarded everything logged during manual operation, and registered each cycle onto a common domain with cubic spline smoothing, so cycles of different durations could be compared as curves.
Finding the faults. Treating each cycle as a function rather than a pile of points let us use tools from functional data analysis. For each curve we computed two outlyingness measures, one capturing how far its level sits from the typical cycle and one capturing how unusual its variability is. Plotting those pairs and drawing a bagplot — a two-dimensional generalization of the boxplot — isolates cycles that behave unlike their neighbors. Those are the candidate faults, and they showed up as visibly abnormal pressure curves when we went back and looked. Because the operators kept records, we could check the flags against what had actually happened to ensure that the method was catching real faults. Several corresponded to logged events: a day a valve was left running after manual operation, a session where a sensor failed mid-run.



Visualization. Synthetic cycles standing in for the real sensor record. Top: each operating cycle between backwashes, registered onto a common domain so cycles of different lengths can be compared as curves. Bottom: outlyingness metrics for each curve, with the bag covering the innermost half of cycles and the dashed fence marking the outlier boundary. Cycles outside the fence are the candidate faults.


We closed by recommending clustering as the next step, with early results using the Calinski-Harabasz criterion suggesting it would catch faults the bagplot approach missed.

Joint work with two other fellows, with faculty support from both institutions. Published as a program technical brief.

title: Kaylee Pascarella
text:
PhD Statistics · Austin, Texas


I’m a PhD statistician recently graduated from Baylor University. Most of my training is in Bayesian methods and clinical trial estimands. My favorite part of the work is that it’s collaborative: the interesting problems arrive from someone else, in someone else’s language, and I get to use my statistical background to help solve them.

I defended my PhD in Statistics at Baylor University in July 2026, advised by Dr. John W. Seaman Jr. My dissertation developed Bayesian methods for two stages of drug development: analyzing composite strategy estimands in confirmatory trials, and estimating drug exposure in preclinical studies where each animal contributes only a single measurement.
Alongside the methodology, I have spent several years doing applied work. I interned with AstraZeneca’s Late Respiratory and Immunology statistics group, giving me exposure to the real clinical trial process and its common problems. I have supported clinical research at Baylor Scott & White Health, and I consulted through Baylor’s Statistical Consulting Center on problems ranging from municipal infrastructure to public health. I work mainly in R, alongside SAS and Python.
